stem: A measure of central tendency is a single value that:
options: represents/summarises the whole set of data by giving a central or typical value around which the data cluster
solution: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents or summarises a whole set of data — by giving a central, typical, or representative value around which the data tend to cluster/concentrate. It is a way of describing the 'centre' or 'average' of the data with one number (instead of the whole mass of figures). The main measures of central tendency are the mean (average), the median (middle value), and the mode (most frequent value). These 'averages' condense the data into a single representative figure that is easy to understand and compare. Understanding what a measure of central tendency is is a key prelims-relevant point. A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents/summarises the data by giving a central, typical value around which the data cluster.

stem: The three main measures of central tendency (averages) are the mean, the median, and the:
solution: The three main measures of central tendency (types of 'average') are: (1) the mean (the arithmetic average — the sum of all the values divided by the number of values); (2) the median (the middle value, when the data are arranged in order); and (3) the mode (the value that occurs most frequently). Each represents the 'centre' of the data in a different way, and each is useful in different situations. (Along with these three, the geometric mean and harmonic mean are other, less common, averages.) So the three main averages are the mean, median, and mode. Understanding the three main measures of central tendency is a key prelims-relevant point. The three main measures of central tendency are the mean, the median, and the mode.

stem: The (arithmetic) mean of a set of values is calculated by:
options: adding up all the values and dividing by the number of values
subtracting the smallest from the largest
solution: The (arithmetic) mean — the most common 'average' — of a set of values is calculated by adding up all the values (finding their sum/total) and then dividing by the number of values (observations). In symbols: mean = (sum of all the values) ÷ (number of values), often written as x̄ = Σx ÷ N. For example, the mean of 4, 6, and 8 is (4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 3 = 18 ÷ 3 = 6. The arithmetic mean uses all the values and is the most widely-used measure of central tendency. Understanding how to compute the mean is a key prelims-relevant point. The (arithmetic) mean is calculated by adding up all the values and dividing by the number of values.

stem: The mean of the values 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 is:
solution: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. Sum = 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50 = 150. Number of values = 5. Mean = 150 ÷ 5 = 30. So the mean of these five values is 30. Understanding how to compute a mean (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. The mean of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 is 150 ÷ 5 = 30.

stem: The median of a set of data is:
options: the middle value, when the data are arranged in order (ascending or descending)
solution: The median of a set of data is the middle value — the value that lies exactly in the middle when the data are arranged in order (ascending or descending order of magnitude). It divides the data into two equal halves: half of the values are below the median, and half are above it. For an odd number of values, the median is the single middle value; for an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values. The median is a positional average (based on position, not on all the values), and it is not affected by extreme values. Understanding the median (the middle value) is a key prelims-relevant point. The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order.

stem: The median of the data 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 (already in order) is:
solution: To find the median, arrange the data in order (here they are already in ascending order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and find the middle value. There are 5 values (an odd number), so the median is the single middle value — the 3rd value: 3, 5, [7], 9, 11. So the median is 7. (It divides the data into two halves: 3 and 5 below it, and 9 and 11 above it.) Understanding how to find the median (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. The median of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 is the middle value, 7.

stem: When there is an EVEN number of values, the median is:
options: the average (mean) of the two middle values
solution: When a data set has an even number of values, there is no single middle value — instead there are two middle values. In that case, the median is taken as the average (arithmetic mean) of these two middle values. For example, for the data 4, 6, 8, 10 (four values, in order), the two middle values are 6 and 8, so the median = (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7. (For an odd number of values, the median is simply the single middle value.) Understanding how to find the median for an even number of values is a prelims-relevant point. For an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle values.

stem: The mode of a set of data is:
options: the value that occurs most frequently (the most common value)
solution: The mode of a set of data is the value that occurs most frequently — i.e., the value that appears the greatest number of times in the data (the most common/most typical value). For example, in the data 2, 3, 3, 5, 3, 7, the mode is 3 (it occurs three times, more than any other value). The mode represents the most usual/popular value. (A data set can sometimes have more than one mode — bimodal or multimodal — or no mode at all if no value repeats.) The mode is especially useful for qualitative data and for finding the most common item. Understanding the mode (most frequent value) is a key prelims-relevant point. The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in the data.

stem: The mode of the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 8, 8 is:
solution: The mode is the value that occurs most frequently. In the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 8, 8: the value 4 occurs three times, the value 8 occurs twice, and the values 2 and 6 occur once each. So 4 occurs the most often (three times) — the mode is 4. Understanding how to find the mode (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. The mode of 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 8, 8 is 4 (it occurs most frequently).

stem: A major ADVANTAGE of the arithmetic mean is that it:
options: is based on all the values (uses every observation) and is easy to calculate and understand
is the same as the mode
solution: A major advantage of the arithmetic mean is that it is based on all the values in the data — it uses/takes into account every single observation (since it sums them all) — so it fully represents the whole data set. It is also easy to understand and to calculate, it is precisely defined, and it is suitable for further algebraic/statistical treatment (calculations). Because it uses all the data and is well-defined, the mean is the most widely used and generally the most reliable average (in many situations). (Its main disadvantage is that it is affected by extreme values.) Understanding this advantage of the mean (uses all values, easy to compute) is a prelims-relevant point. A major advantage of the mean is that it is based on all the values and is easy to calculate and understand.

stem: A major DISADVANTAGE of the arithmetic mean is that it is:
options: greatly affected (distorted) by extreme values (very high or very low values)
solution: A major disadvantage of the arithmetic mean is that it is greatly affected (distorted/pulled) by extreme values — that is, by unusually high or unusually low values in the data. Because the mean uses all the values (including the extremes), a single very large (or very small) value can pull the mean up (or down) away from the 'typical' centre of the data, making it unrepresentative. For example, if most people in a group earn modest incomes but one person is a billionaire, the mean income would be pulled up high and would not represent the typical person. (In such cases, the median — which is not affected by extremes — is a better measure.) Understanding this disadvantage of the mean (affected by extremes) is a key prelims-relevant point. A major disadvantage of the mean is that it is greatly affected/distorted by extreme (very high or very low) values.

stem: When a data set has extreme values (outliers), a BETTER measure of central tendency (one not affected by extremes) is the:
solution: When a data set has extreme values (outliers — a few unusually high or low values), a better measure of central tendency than the mean is the median. This is because the median is a positional average — it is simply the middle value (based on position, not on the actual magnitudes of the extreme values) — so it is NOT affected/distorted by extreme values. For example, in a set of incomes where most are modest but one is enormous, the median gives a more representative 'typical' value than the mean (which the huge income would pull up). So the median is preferred when there are extreme values (or open-ended/skewed data). Understanding that the median is better with extreme values is a key prelims-relevant point. When there are extreme values, the median is a better measure of central tendency, because it is not affected by extremes.

stem: The measure of central tendency MOST suitable for QUALITATIVE data (like the most popular shoe size, or the most common colour) is the:
solution: The measure of central tendency most suitable for qualitative data — and for finding the most common/popular item — is the mode. This is because the mode is simply the most frequently occurring value/category, which can be found even for qualitative data (attributes), where the mean and median cannot be meaningfully calculated. For example, to find the most popular shoe size sold, the most common colour of cars, or the most preferred brand, we use the mode (the item that occurs most often). So the mode is the appropriate average for qualitative/categorical data and for identifying the most typical/popular item. Understanding that the mode suits qualitative data is a prelims-relevant point. The mode is the measure of central tendency most suitable for qualitative data (like the most popular size or most common item).

stem: The median is a __________ average, because it is determined by the POSITION of the values (not by their actual magnitudes).
solution: The median is a positional average, because it is determined by the position of the values in the ordered data (specifically, the value at the middle position) — NOT by the actual magnitudes of all the values. To find the median, we arrange the data in order and pick out the middle value (by its position); the exact values of the other observations (especially the extremes) do not affect it. This is why the median is not affected by extreme values. (The mode is also a positional/locational average — determined by where the values concentrate. The mean, by contrast, is a 'calculated'/mathematical average, using the actual magnitudes of all the values.) Understanding that the median is a positional average is a prelims-relevant point. The median is a positional average, determined by the position of the values (not their actual magnitudes).

stem: For a moderately (symmetrically) distributed data set, the mean, median, and mode are:
options: equal (or approximately equal) to each other
solution: For a perfectly symmetrical (bell-shaped/normal) distribution, the mean, median, and mode are all equal to each other (they coincide at the centre). For a moderately/approximately symmetrical distribution, they are approximately equal (close together). (When the distribution is skewed — asymmetrical — they separate: the mean is pulled toward the tail/extreme values, the mode is at the peak, and the median lies in between. An approximate relationship for moderately skewed distributions is: Mode ≈ 3 × Median − 2 × Mean.) So, the more symmetrical the data, the closer the three averages are; for a symmetrical distribution they are equal. Understanding this (mean = median = mode for symmetrical data) is a prelims-relevant point. For a symmetrical distribution, the mean, median, and mode are equal (or approximately equal).

stem: The mode is especially useful in business (e.g., for a shoe or garment shop) for finding:
options: the most demanded/popular size or item (the one that sells the most), so as to stock more of it
solution: The mode is especially useful in business (like a shoe shop, garment shop, or any retail business) for finding the most demanded/popular size or item — the size, style, or product that sells the most (occurs most frequently in the sales/demand). Knowing the mode (the most common size/item) helps the business decide what to stock more of (produce or order the most-demanded sizes/items in larger quantities) and how to plan its inventory — which is more useful for this purpose than the mean or median. So the mode's ability to identify the most frequent/popular item makes it valuable in business and marketing decisions. Understanding this practical use of the mode is a prelims-relevant point. The mode helps businesses find the most demanded/popular size or item (the best-selling one), so as to stock more of it.

stem: The __________ mean is a special average used to find the average rate of growth over time (like an average growth rate of population or investment).
solution: The geometric mean (GM) is a special type of average used especially to find the average rate of growth/change over time — such as the average annual rate of growth of population, prices, investment, or production. It is calculated by taking the nth root of the product of n values (rather than summing and dividing, as the arithmetic mean does). The geometric mean is the appropriate average for rates of growth, ratios, and percentages that compound over time (because growth is multiplicative). So, for average growth rates, the geometric mean (not the arithmetic mean) is used. Understanding the geometric mean (for average growth rates) is a prelims-relevant point. The geometric mean is used to find the average rate of growth over time (like an average growth rate).

stem: A 'weighted mean' is used instead of a simple mean when:
options: different values have different importance/weights (so each is weighted by its importance before averaging)
solution: A weighted mean (weighted average) is used instead of a simple (unweighted) mean when the different values do NOT have equal importance — that is, when some values are more important than others (they should count for more). In the weighted mean, each value is multiplied by a 'weight' representing its importance, and then the sum of these products is divided by the sum of the weights. For example, if a student's marks in different subjects have different credit-weights, or if items in a price index have different importance, a weighted mean is appropriate. So the weighted mean accounts for the differing importance of the values. (The simple mean is just a weighted mean with all weights equal.) Understanding the weighted mean is a prelims-relevant point. A weighted mean is used when different values have different importance (weights), so each is weighted by its importance before averaging.

stem: An ideal/good measure of central tendency should be well-defined, based on all observations, easy to understand, and:
options: not unduly affected by extreme values, and capable of further mathematical treatment
solution: An ideal (good) measure of central tendency should have several desirable properties: it should be rigidly/clearly defined (so everyone computes it the same way, with no ambiguity); based on all the observations (using all the data); easy to understand and to calculate; not unduly affected by extreme values (so it stays representative even with outliers); capable of further algebraic/mathematical treatment (usable in further calculations); and stable (not fluctuating much from sample to sample). No single average has all these properties perfectly — for example, the mean uses all values and allows further treatment but is affected by extremes; the median is not affected by extremes but does not use all values and is less suited to further math. So the choice of average depends on the situation. Understanding the properties of a good average is a prelims-relevant point. A good measure of central tendency should be well-defined, based on all observations, easy to understand, not unduly affected by extremes, and capable of further mathematical treatment.

stem: Assertion (A): The median is preferred over the mean for a data set of incomes that includes a few extremely high incomes. Reason (R): The mean is pulled up by the extreme high values, while the median (the middle value) is not affected by them. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the median is preferred over the mean for a data set of incomes that includes a few extremely high incomes. And the reason is (R) that the mean is pulled up (distorted) by those extreme high values (since it sums all the values, the huge incomes drag the average upward, making it unrepresentative of the typical person), whereas the median — being simply the middle value (a positional average) — is NOT affected by the extreme values. So, because the median resists the distortion caused by the extreme incomes (while the mean does not), the median gives a more representative 'typical' income — which is exactly why it is preferred here. So R correctly explains A. Understanding this (median preferred with extreme values, because the mean is distorted) is a key prelims-relevant point. The median is preferred with extreme incomes because the mean is pulled up by the high values, while the median is not affected by them.

stem: For a grouped/discrete frequency distribution, the mean is calculated as __________ (where f = frequency, x = value/midpoint).
options: Σfx ÷ Σf (sum of frequency×value, divided by total frequency)
solution: For a grouped (or discrete) frequency distribution, the mean is calculated as: mean (x̄) = Σfx ÷ Σf — that is, multiply each value (x) — for a continuous series, the class midpoint — by its frequency (f), add up all these products (Σfx), and divide by the total frequency (Σf, i.e., N, the total number of observations). This weights each value by how often it occurs. For example, if the value 5 occurs 3 times and 8 occurs 2 times, the mean = (5×3 + 8×2) ÷ (3+2) = (15+16) ÷ 5 = 31 ÷ 5 = 6.2. This 'direct method' formula (Σfx ÷ Σf) is the basic way to find the mean of frequency data. Understanding this formula is a prelims-relevant point. For a frequency distribution, the mean = Σfx ÷ Σf (sum of frequency×value, divided by total frequency).

stem: In calculating the mean of a continuous (grouped) frequency distribution, the value 'x' used for each class is the class:
solution: In calculating the mean of a continuous (grouped) frequency distribution, the value 'x' used to represent each class is the class midpoint (mid-value) — the average of the class's lower and upper limits. This is because, once data are grouped into classes, the individual values are lost, so the midpoint is taken as the representative/typical value of all the observations in that class. Then the mean is found as Σfx ÷ Σf, using these midpoints as x. (This introduces some approximation, since not all values in a class actually equal the midpoint — this is part of the 'loss of information' from grouping.) Understanding that the class midpoint is used as x for the mean is a prelims-relevant point. In finding the mean of a continuous frequency distribution, the class midpoint (mid-value) is used as the value 'x' for each class.

stem: A property of the arithmetic mean is that the SUM of the deviations of all the values from the mean is always:
solution: A key mathematical property of the arithmetic mean is that the sum of the deviations of all the values from the mean is always equal to zero — that is, Σ(x − x̄) = 0. This is because the mean is the 'balancing point' (centre of gravity) of the data: the positive deviations (of values above the mean) exactly cancel out the negative deviations (of values below the mean). For example, for the values 4, 6, 8 with mean 6: the deviations are (4−6) + (6−6) + (8−6) = −2 + 0 + 2 = 0. This property (deviations from the mean sum to zero) is a defining characteristic of the mean. Understanding this property is a prelims-relevant point. A property of the arithmetic mean is that the sum of the deviations of all the values from the mean is always zero.

stem: The 'assumed mean method' (and 'step-deviation method') are used to calculate the mean:
options: more easily/quickly (by simplifying the arithmetic), especially when the values are large
solution: The 'assumed mean method' and the 'step-deviation method' are shortcut methods used to calculate the arithmetic mean more easily and quickly — by simplifying the arithmetic — especially when the values (or their frequencies) are large or awkward to work with directly. In the assumed mean method, an approximate/convenient value is 'assumed' as a temporary mean, the deviations of the actual values from this assumed mean are computed (which are smaller, easier numbers), and then a correction is applied to get the true mean. The step-deviation method goes further by also dividing the deviations by the common class width (a common factor), making the numbers even smaller and the calculation still easier. Both methods give exactly the same result as the direct method — they just make the computation easier. Understanding these shortcut methods is a prelims-relevant point. The assumed mean and step-deviation methods are shortcuts to calculate the mean more easily, especially with large values.

stem: The position of the median in an ordered data set of N items is generally given by the __________ item.
solution: The position of the median in an ordered data set (individual series) of N items is given by the (N+1)/2 th item — i.e., after arranging the data in order, the median is the value at the (N+1)/2 position. For example, if N = 5, the median is the (5+1)/2 = 3rd item (the middle one); if N = 7, it is the 4th item. (For an even N, (N+1)/2 gives a position between two items — e.g., for N = 6 it gives 3.5 — meaning the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th items.) So (N+1)/2 locates the median's position. Understanding the median-position formula is a prelims-relevant point. The position of the median is given by the (N+1)/2 th item in the ordered data.

stem: The values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts are called:
solution: Quartiles are the values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts (quarters). There are three quartiles: the first quartile (Q1, the 'lower quartile') — below which lies the lowest 25% of the data; the second quartile (Q2) — which is the same as the median (below which lies 50% of the data); and the third quartile (Q3, the 'upper quartile') — below which lies 75% of the data. Quartiles are 'partition values' (like the median, they are positional measures that divide the data). (Similarly, deciles divide the data into 10 parts, and percentiles into 100 parts.) Understanding quartiles is a prelims-relevant point. Quartiles are the values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts (Q1, Q2 = median, Q3).

stem: The second quartile (Q2), the fifth decile (D5), and the fiftieth percentile (P50) are all equal to the:
solution: The second quartile (Q2), the fifth decile (D5), and the fiftieth percentile (P50) are all equal to the median. This is because all of these are the value that divides the data set so that 50% of the observations lie below it (and 50% above) — which is exactly the definition of the median. Q2 is the value below which lies 2/4 = 50% of the data; D5 is the value below which lies 5/10 = 50%; and P50 is the value below which lies 50/100 = 50%. So Q2 = D5 = P50 = the median (all mark the middle/50% point). Understanding this equivalence is a prelims-relevant point. The second quartile (Q2), the fifth decile (D5), and the fiftieth percentile (P50) are all equal to the median.

stem: Values that divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts are called:
solution: Percentiles are the values that divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts. There are 99 percentiles (P1, P2, ..., P99): the pth percentile is the value below which p% of the observations fall. For example, P25 (the 25th percentile) is the value below which 25% of the data lie (= Q1, the first quartile), and P50 (the 50th percentile) = the median. Percentiles are widely used to describe relative standing (e.g., a student scoring in the 90th percentile did better than 90% of the others). (Similarly: quartiles divide into 4 parts, deciles into 10 parts.) Understanding percentiles is a prelims-relevant point. Percentiles are the values that divide an ordered data set into 100 equal parts.

stem: Values that divide an ordered data set into 10 equal parts are called:
solution: Deciles are the values that divide an ordered data set into 10 equal parts. There are 9 deciles (D1, D2, ..., D9): the kth decile is the value below which (k × 10)% of the observations fall. For example, D1 (the first decile) is the value below which the lowest 10% of the data lie, and D5 (the fifth decile) = the median (below which 50% lie). Deciles are 'partition values' like the quartiles and percentiles. (Quartiles divide into 4 parts; deciles into 10; percentiles into 100.) Understanding deciles is a prelims-relevant point. Deciles are the values that divide an ordered data set into 10 equal parts.

stem: Quartiles, deciles, and percentiles (along with the median) are collectively known as __________ values.
solution: Quartiles, deciles, and percentiles — along with the median — are collectively known as partition values (or positional values). This is because they are positional measures that partition (divide) the ordered data set into a number of equal parts: the median divides it into 2 equal halves; the quartiles into 4 parts; the deciles into 10 parts; and the percentiles into 100 parts. They all describe the position/location of values within the distribution (rather than being calculated from all the values like the mean). Understanding that these are collectively partition values is a prelims-relevant point. Quartiles, deciles, and percentiles (with the median) are collectively known as partition (positional) values.

stem: In a POSITIVELY skewed distribution (a long tail toward the high values), the relationship among the averages is:
solution: In a positively skewed distribution (asymmetrical, with a long tail extending toward the higher/right-hand values), the relationship among the three averages is: Mean > Median > Mode. This is because the few high extreme values in the long right tail pull the mean up (toward the high values) the most, the mode stays at the peak (the most frequent value, toward the lower end), and the median lies in between. So the mean is the largest, the mode the smallest, and the median in the middle. (In a negatively skewed distribution, the order reverses: Mean < Median < Mode. And in a symmetrical distribution, Mean = Median = Mode.) Understanding this relationship for positive skew is a prelims-relevant point. In a positively skewed distribution, Mean > Median > Mode.

stem: In a NEGATIVELY skewed distribution (a long tail toward the low values), the relationship among the averages is:
solution: In a negatively skewed distribution (asymmetrical, with a long tail extending toward the lower/left-hand values), the relationship among the three averages is: Mean < Median < Mode. This is because the few low extreme values in the long left tail pull the mean down (toward the low values) the most, while the mode stays at the peak (toward the higher end) and the median lies in between. So here the mean is the smallest, the mode the largest, and the median in the middle — the reverse of the positively-skewed case. (For a symmetrical distribution, Mean = Median = Mode.) Understanding this relationship for negative skew is a prelims-relevant point. In a negatively skewed distribution, Mean < Median < Mode.

stem: The empirical (approximate) relationship among the three averages for a moderately skewed distribution is: Mode = 3 Median − __________.
solution: The empirical (approximate) relationship among the mean, median, and mode for a moderately (asymmetrically) skewed distribution is: Mode = 3 × Median − 2 × Mean. This useful empirical formula (given by Karl Pearson) lets us estimate any one of the three averages if the other two are known — for example, if the mean and median are known, the mode can be estimated. (It reflects the fact that, in a moderately skewed distribution, the median lies about one-third of the way from the mean to the mode.) For a symmetrical distribution (where all three are equal), the relationship also holds trivially. Understanding this empirical relationship (Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean) is a prelims-relevant point. The empirical relationship is: Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean (for a moderately skewed distribution).

stem: A DISADVANTAGE of the median is that:
options: it is affected by extreme values
it is not based on all the values (it ignores the actual magnitudes of most observations) and is not well suited to further algebraic treatment
it cannot be found for ordered data
solution: A disadvantage of the median is that it is NOT based on all the values of the data — it depends only on the middle value (its position), and it ignores the actual magnitudes of most of the other observations (especially the extremes). Because it does not use all the data, it can be less representative in some cases, and it is not well suited to further algebraic/mathematical treatment (e.g., you cannot easily combine medians of different groups the way you can combine means). (Its main advantages, on the other hand, are that it is simple, not affected by extreme values, and can be found for open-ended distributions.) So a key limitation of the median is that it ignores most of the values and is not amenable to further algebra. Understanding the disadvantages of the median is a prelims-relevant point. A disadvantage of the median is that it is not based on all the values and is not well suited to further algebraic treatment.

stem: An ADVANTAGE of the median (and mode) over the mean is that they CAN be determined even for an __________ frequency distribution (with open-ended classes like 'below 10' or 'above 90').
solution: An advantage of the median (and the mode) over the mean is that they can be determined even for an open-ended frequency distribution — one with open-ended classes such as 'below 10' or 'above 90' (classes with no lower or no upper limit). This is because the median and mode depend on the position/location of values (the middle, or the most frequent class), not on the exact values in the open-ended end classes. The mean, by contrast, cannot be directly calculated for open-ended classes, because it needs the midpoints (exact values) of ALL the classes, and an open-ended class has no defined midpoint. So, for open-ended distributions, the median or mode is used (not the mean). Understanding this advantage (median/mode work for open-ended data) is a prelims-relevant point. The median (and mode) can be determined even for open-ended frequency distributions, whereas the mean cannot.

stem: The harmonic mean is a special average used for averaging __________ (like average speed when equal distances are covered at different speeds).
solution: The harmonic mean (HM) is a special type of average used for averaging rates and ratios — particularly in situations like finding the average speed when equal distances are covered at different speeds, or averaging rates such as price per unit. The harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the values. It gives more weight to the smaller values, and it is the appropriate average when the values are rates defined per unit of something (like km per hour) and we are averaging over equal amounts of the 'something' (like equal distances). For example, if you travel one distance at 40 km/h and an equal distance at 60 km/h, the average speed for the whole trip is the harmonic mean of 40 and 60 (which is 48), not the arithmetic mean (50). Understanding the harmonic mean (for averaging rates) is a prelims-relevant point. The harmonic mean is used for averaging rates/ratios (like average speed over equal distances at different speeds).

stem: The 'combined mean' of two groups (with different means and sizes) is found by:
options: taking a weighted average of the two group means (weighted by the number of items in each group)
solution: The combined mean of two (or more) groups — the mean of all the items of the groups taken together — is found by taking a weighted average of the individual group means, weighted by the number of items (sizes) in each group. In formula: combined mean = (N1·x̄1 + N2·x̄2) ÷ (N1 + N2), where N1, N2 are the sizes and x̄1, x̄2 the means of the two groups. (It is essentially the total of all the values, divided by the total number of items.) It is NOT correct to simply average the two means (unless the two groups happen to be of equal size) — the larger group must count for more. So the combined mean weights each group's mean by its size. Understanding the combined mean (weighted by group sizes) is a prelims-relevant point. The combined mean of two groups is a weighted average of their means, weighted by the number of items in each group.

stem: Which average CANNOT be calculated for purely qualitative data (like colours or brands)?
options: the arithmetic mean and the median (they need numerical/orderable data)
solution: For purely qualitative data that cannot be measured or even ordered/ranked (like colours, brands, or religions), the arithmetic mean CANNOT be calculated (there are no numbers to add up and average), and the median also cannot be meaningfully found (the data cannot be arranged in a numerical/ordered sequence to find a 'middle' value). Only the mode can be found — the most frequently occurring category (e.g., the most common colour). (Note: for qualitative data that CAN be ranked/ordered — 'ordinal' data, like grades A/B/C — the median can sometimes be found by rank, but not the mean.) So for unordered qualitative data, the mode is the only usable average. Understanding this (mean and median can't be used for unordered qualitative data; only mode can) is a prelims-relevant point. For purely qualitative data (like colours/brands), the arithmetic mean and median cannot be calculated — only the mode can.

stem: A DISADVANTAGE of the mode is that:
options: it is always unique and clear
it may be ill-defined (a data set can have no mode, or more than one mode) and it is not based on all the values
solution: A disadvantage of the mode is that it may be ill-defined/indeterminate: a data set can sometimes have no mode (if no value repeats — all values occur equally often) or more than one mode (bimodal or multimodal — if two or more values tie for the highest frequency), making the mode ambiguous or not unique. Also, the mode is not based on all the values (it depends only on the most frequent value/class, ignoring the rest), and it is not well suited to further algebraic treatment. (Its advantages: it is simple, easily understood, not affected by extreme values, and suitable for qualitative data and finding the most popular item.) Understanding the disadvantages of the mode is a prelims-relevant point. A disadvantage of the mode is that it may be ill-defined (no mode, or more than one mode) and is not based on all the values.

stem: In a grouped frequency distribution, the class with the highest frequency (used to locate the mode) is called the __________ class.
solution: In a grouped frequency distribution, the 'modal class' is the class (class interval) that has the highest frequency — i.e., the class into which the greatest number of observations fall. Since the mode is the most frequently occurring value, it lies within this modal class. To find the exact value of the mode in a continuous distribution, a formula (interpolation formula) is applied using the frequency of the modal class and those of the classes just before and after it. So the modal class is the first thing identified when finding the mode of grouped data (it locates where the mode is). Understanding the modal class is a prelims-relevant point. In a grouped frequency distribution, the modal class is the class with the highest frequency (where the mode lies).

stem: The mean is the ONLY common average that lends itself well to further __________ (algebraic) treatment (like combining group means).
solution: The mean (arithmetic mean) is the only one of the common averages that lends itself well to further mathematical/algebraic treatment. Because the mean is calculated using all the values in a definite algebraic way (Σx ÷ N), it can be used in further calculations and manipulations — for example, the means of different groups can be combined into a single 'combined mean' (a weighted average), and the mean is used in many further statistical formulas (like those for standard deviation, correlation, etc.). The median and mode, being positional averages (not using all the values algebraically), do not lend themselves to such further mathematical treatment. This 'amenability to further algebra' is a distinctive advantage of the mean. Understanding this is a prelims-relevant point. The mean is the only common average that lends itself well to further mathematical/algebraic treatment (like combining group means).

stem: For an ordered individual series with an ODD number of observations, the median is:
options: the average of the two middle values
solution: For an ordered individual series (data arranged in order) with an odd number of observations (N is odd), the median is simply the single middle value — the value at the (N+1)/2 position. For example, for 7 values in order, the median is the (7+1)/2 = 4th value (the exact middle one), with 3 values below it and 3 above it. (Only when N is even are there two middle values, whose average is then taken as the median.) So for an odd N, the median is the lone middle value. Understanding this is a prelims-relevant point. For an odd number of observations, the median is simply the single middle value (at the (N+1)/2 position).

stem: The third quartile (Q3) is the value below which lies __________ of the data.
solution: The third quartile (Q3, the 'upper quartile') is the value below which lies 75% of the data (three-quarters of the observations) — and above which lies the top 25%. (For comparison: Q1, the first/lower quartile, has 25% of the data below it; Q2, the second quartile = the median, has 50% below it; and Q3 has 75% below it.) So Q3 marks off the highest quarter of the data. Understanding what Q3 represents (75% below it) is a prelims-relevant point. The third quartile (Q3) is the value below which lies 75% of the data.

stem: A situation where the MEDIAN is the most appropriate average is when the data are __________ (can be ranked) but the distances between ranks are not meaningful.
solution: The median is the most appropriate average when the data are ordinal/ranked — that is, when the items can be arranged in order/ranked (like grades A, B, C, D; or levels of satisfaction; or preferences from 1st to last), but the 'distances' between the ranks are not numerically meaningful (the gap between A and B is not a measurable quantity). In such cases, the mean cannot be meaningfully calculated (there are no true numerical values to average), but the median CAN be found — as the middle rank/category (the value of the middle-ranked item). So for ranked/ordinal data, the median is the suitable average. (The mode could also be used, but the median gives the central/middle rank.) Understanding this use of the median (for ordinal/ranked data) is a prelims-relevant point. The median is the most appropriate average for ordinal/ranked data (which can be ranked but whose rank-distances are not meaningful).

stem: The mean of a discrete series with values 2, 4, 6 having frequencies 1, 2, 3 respectively is:
solution: For a discrete frequency series, the mean = Σfx ÷ Σf. Here the values (x) are 2, 4, 6 with frequencies (f) 1, 2, 3. Compute Σfx = (2×1) + (4×2) + (6×3) = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28. And Σf = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. So mean = 28 ÷ 6 ≈ 4.67. Understanding how to compute the mean of a discrete series (with this example) is a prelims-relevant point. The mean = Σfx ÷ Σf = 28 ÷ 6 ≈ 4.67.

stem: Which measure of central tendency would best describe the 'typical' size of a family in a locality where a few very large joint families exist among many small families?
options: the mean (which the large families would inflate)
the median or mode (not distorted by the few very large families)
solution: In a locality with many small families but a few very large joint families, the median or the mode would best describe the 'typical' family size — because these measures are not distorted by the few very large (extreme) families. The mean, by contrast, would be inflated (pulled up) by the few very large families, giving a figure larger than the size of most (typical) families — so it would be misleading. The median (the middle family size) or the mode (the most common family size) would better represent the size of a typical family. This illustrates choosing the average to suit the data (median/mode when there are extreme values). Understanding this application is a prelims-relevant point. The median or mode best describes the typical family size here, because they are not distorted by the few very large families (unlike the mean).

stem: The mean, median, and mode are all types of averages, but the mean is specifically the __________ average.
solution: The mean, median, and mode are all 'averages' (measures of central tendency), but they are different types: the mean is the arithmetic (calculated) average — it is computed using the actual magnitudes of all the values (summing them and dividing). The median is a positional average (the middle value, by position), and the mode is also a positional/locational average (the most frequently occurring value, by location of concentration). So, of the three, the mean is the true 'mathematical'/calculated average (using all the values arithmetically), while the median and mode are positional averages. Understanding that the mean is the arithmetic/calculated average is a prelims-relevant point. The mean is the arithmetic (calculated) average, using all the values, whereas the median and mode are positional averages.

stem: The choice of which measure of central tendency to use depends on:
options: the nature of the data (quantitative/qualitative, presence of extreme values, open-ended classes) and the purpose of the study
solution: The choice of which measure of central tendency (mean, median, or mode) to use depends on the nature of the data and the purpose of the study. Considerations include: whether the data are quantitative or qualitative (the mean and median need numerical/orderable data, while the mode can handle qualitative data); whether there are extreme values/outliers (if so, the median is better than the mean); whether the distribution has open-ended classes (then the median or mode, not the mean); whether all the values should be used (the mean) or a positional/typical value is wanted (median or mode); whether further algebraic treatment is needed (the mean); and what exactly we want to represent (average, middle, or most common). So no single average is best for every situation — the appropriate one is chosen to fit the data and the purpose. Understanding this (choice depends on data and purpose) is a key prelims-relevant point. The choice of average depends on the nature of the data (quantitative/qualitative, extreme values, open-ended classes) and the purpose of the study.

stem: Assertion (A): The mode is the most suitable average for finding the most fashionable/popular item. Reason (R): The mode is the value/item that occurs most frequently in the data. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the mode is the most suitable average for finding the most fashionable/popular item (e.g., the most popular size, style, brand, or product). And the reason is (R) that the mode is, by definition, the value/item that occurs most frequently in the data — i.e., the most common one. Since 'most popular/fashionable' means exactly 'occurring most frequently/most in demand', the mode (the most frequent value) is precisely what identifies it. So R correctly explains why the mode is the suitable average for the most popular item (A). (This is why the mode is valued in business/marketing.) Understanding this is a prelims-relevant point. The mode is best for finding the most popular item because it is the value/item that occurs most frequently.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Measures of Central Tendency' is that:
options: A measure of central tendency (an 'average') summarises a whole data set with a single representative central value — the mean (average of all values), the median (the middle value), and the mode (the most frequent value) — each with its own method, advantages, and limitations, so that the appropriate average is chosen according to the nature of the data and the purpose
Only the mean should ever be used
solution: The chapter conveys that a measure of central tendency (an 'average') is a single value that represents/summarises a whole set of data by a central, typical value around which the data cluster — condensing a mass of figures into one representative number. It explains the three main measures of central tendency: (1) the mean (arithmetic mean/average) — the sum of all the values divided by their number — which uses all the observations and is easy to compute and widely used, but is greatly affected/distorted by extreme values; (2) the median — the middle value when the data are arranged in order — a positional average that divides the data into two equal halves and is NOT affected by extreme values (so it is preferred for data with extreme/outlier values or open-ended, skewed distributions); and (3) the mode — the most frequently occurring value — which identifies the most common/popular value and is especially useful for qualitative data and in business (finding the most-demanded item/size). It discusses how to calculate each (for individual, discrete, and continuous data), their respective advantages and disadvantages, the properties of an ideal average, related measures (like the weighted mean and the geometric mean, used for growth rates), and the relationship among the mean, median, and mode (equal for symmetrical distributions, and separating with skewness). The key lesson is that each average has its uses and limitations, so the appropriate measure of central tendency must be chosen according to the nature of the data and the purpose of the study. Understanding what averages are, how to compute the mean, median, and mode, and when to use each is the central concern of this chapter. A measure of central tendency summarises the data with one representative value — the mean, median, or mode — each with its own method, merits, and limits, so the right average is chosen to suit the data and purpose.
